nameStory: The 'cutleaf' part of this flower's name comes from its deeply divided, almost lacy leaves that look like they've been cut with scissors. The 'coneflower' refers to the prominent green or yellowish center that rises up like a little cone from the middle of the bright yellow petals.
description: Cutleaf coneflower is a tall, cheerful wildflower that can tower over you at 3-10 feet high. It produces clusters of bright yellow daisy-like flowers with drooping petals surrounding a distinctive greenish cone-shaped center. The plant gets its name from its deeply divided, almost feathery leaves that give it a delicate, lacy appearance despite its impressive height.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are deeply cut into narrow, finger-like segments that feel smooth to the touch and create an almost fern-like appearance - this intricate leaf cutting is unique among local coneflowers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 6-10 drooping petals surrounding a greenish or yellowish dome-shaped center that feels firm and slightly bumpy when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall and robust, often reaching 6-10 feet with multiple branching stems that form impressive colonies in favorable conditions

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dark seeds develop on the cone center in late summer, creating a bristly texture that birds love to pick at

habitat: Look for cutleaf coneflower in moist, rich soils along stream banks, wet meadows, and woodland edges throughout New England. It thrives in partially shaded areas near water sources and is often found growing alongside jewelweed, cardinal flower, and woodland asters in these damp, fertile spots.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge with distinctive deeply-cut leaves that help identify the plant before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through September with bright yellow flowers creating impressive tall displays.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen on the cone centers while leaves may turn yellow before dying back, and the tall dried stems become visible.
seasonality.winter: Tall, dried brown stems persist through winter, often with seed heads still attached, creating striking silhouettes against snow.

funFact: Despite being toxic to livestock, the young leaves of cutleaf coneflower are actually edible for humans and are traditionally eaten as a cooked green called 'sochan' in Appalachian cuisine - just don't let your pets or farm animals nibble on it!
confusionNotes: The deeply cut, lacy leaves make this nearly impossible to confuse with other coneflowers, which all have simple, uncut leaves. Remember: if the leaves look like they were attacked by scissors, it's cutleaf coneflower!
contextualKnowledge: This plant goes by many names including goldenglow, sochan, and thimbleweed, which can cause confusion since 'thimbleweed' usually refers to a completely different white-flowered plant (Anemone species). The name 'goldenglow' often refers to the double-flowered garden variety.
compareHints: Among the Rudbeckia family, cutleaf coneflower is the giant with the fancy haircut - it's much taller than black-eyed Susan and has those distinctive deeply-divided leaves that no other coneflower possesses. While other coneflowers have simple, whole leaves, this one looks like nature took scissors to every leaf.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, black-eyed Susan is distinguished by its rough, hairy texture and moderate size.
Among the Rudbeckia family, brown-eyed Susan stands out for its smaller flowers and brown (not black) centers.
Orange coneflower differs from black-eyed Susan by forming spreading colonies rather than individual clumps, and has slightly more orange-tinted petals.
Among its Rudbeckia relatives, sweet black-eyed Susan stands out for its impressive height and fragrant flowers.

Great coneflower's towering 8-foot height immediately distinguishes it from all other Rudbeckia species in New England - black-eyed Susan tops out around 3 feet, cutleaf coneflower reaches about 4-6 feet, and orange coneflower stays under 3 feet.
Unlike its Rudbeckia cousins, clasping coneflower has small chaffy scales (like tiny bracts) beneath its ray petals that other black-eyed Susans lack.
